Justification: Required by ISO 27001. Policy approved by management; topic policies (access control, incident response) still being written.

Management approves the policy and alone accepts High and Critical risks. No management review has been held yet.

Subscribe to vendor security advisories (Microsoft, GitHub) and BSI warnings. Low cost, useful for early notice.
Proportionate to a 40-person company: use Microsoft Defender for Cloud alerts and public advisories, no dedicated team.

Files and customer data are sent by email and file sharing. External sharing must be limited to approved domains.
Access to Azure, GitHub, Microsoft 365 and the support tool must follow need-to-know. Sign-in through Entra ID exists, but rules are not written down.
Each person has a unique Entra ID account. The joiner, mover and leaver process is not documented.
Minimum password length is set, but there is no password manager and passwords are still reused.
Access is removed when the IT administrator is told, with no deadline. Rights need regular review.
Payment provider, support tool and backup service handle company or customer data. No supplier register exists.

Justification: StoreSight depends on cloud services and third-party libraries, which are part of the supply chain.

Justification: Key suppliers' security documents must be reviewed at least yearly.

Control name: Information security for use of cloud services
Justification: All core systems run in Azure and Microsoft 365. Responsibility split with Microsoft must be defined and configurations reviewed.

Control name: Information security incident management planning and preparation
Justification: No incident plan exists. Needed for the 24-hour internal reporting objective, 72-hour GDPR deadline and NIS2 timelines.

Control name: Assessment and decision on information security events
Justification: Someone must decide quickly whether an event is an incident and how severe it is.
Defined roles, steps and contact details for containing and recovering from incidents.
Lessons from incidents feed back into the risk register and policies.
Logs and device evidence must be preserved for customer, authority or legal follow-up.
Security controls must stay in place during outages and ransomware recovery.
Recovery time and recovery point targets, and a tested failover plan, are needed for customers who depend on StoreSight.

Control name: Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements
Justification: GDPR applies. NIS2 applicability is not yet assessed. Two enterprise customers have contractual security expectations.
Company uses licensed software and open-source libraries. Licence compliance should be checked with dependency tooling.
ISMS records, contracts and logs must be kept and protected. Support tickets need retention limits.
StoreSight processes customers' personal data, so GDPR duties apply (requests, breaches, protection).
Required by ISO 27001 (internal audit). In a small company this means someone outside the ISMS Manager role.

Justification: Managers check that policies are followed. Open items are reviewed quarterly.
Procedures such as patching, restore tests and leaver steps should be written so more than one person can run them.
Background checks within German law for staff with admin or customer-data access.
Contracts exist, but information security duties are not stated explicitly.

Control name: Information security awareness, education and training
Justification: Phishing is the top risk. Policy objective: annual training for all staff.
Deliberate policy breaches need a defined consequence, using the existing HR process.

Control name: Responsibilities after termination or change of employment
Justification: Leavers stay bound by confidentiality, and role changes trigger an access review.
Staff, contractors and suppliers may see customer data.

No secure areas exist in the office.
Screen-lock guidance covers office and home use. Risk accepted but guidance still given.
No servers or critical equipment on premises. Laptops are covered by 8.1.

USB drives can carry data out of the company.
No critical systems run on premises. Availability of production is handled by Azure.
No on-premises network infrastructure beyond office internet access.
No on-premises equipment to maintain. Laptop lifecycle is covered by 8.1 and 7.14.

Justification: Old or returned laptops must be wiped before re-use or disposal.
All staff have company laptops, and about 12 also read work email on personal phones. No patch deadline or phone rules.
Azure administrator rights are broad, and not all admins use MFA or passkeys.
Access to the database, support tool and Microsoft 365 data must be limited by role.
Source code is StoreSight's core asset. Repositories are private, but MFA is not enforced for every member.
MFA is on email for some staff only. Policy objective: all staff within 3 months, passkeys for admins.
Azure resources must keep up with customer load to avoid outages.
Microsoft Defender antivirus is on laptops, but not centrally monitored.
Windows updates are automatic but not monitored. No patch deadline and no dependency scanning.
Azure and database settings are not reviewed regularly.
Support tickets and customer data need retention limits. GDPR deletion requests must be honoured.
Sensitive data in support tickets should be masked, and test data anonymised.
Unrestricted external sharing and secrets in code are leakage paths.
Backup service exists but restores are never tested and backups are not isolated from ransomware.
Single-region setup. Either add failover or formally accept the risk.
Only basic Azure activity logs. No central logging or retention period.
Attacks can go unnoticed without alerts.
Azure and Microsoft 365 synchronise time by default, which keeps logs reliable.
No on-premises systems with privileged utilities. Cloud admin tools are covered by 8.2.

Control name: Installation of software on operational systems
Justification: Staff-installed software on laptops adds malware and patching risk. Restrict to an approved list.
Database access is not restricted to private endpoints, and remote networks are untrusted.
Network services come from Microsoft and internet providers. Security requirements must be defined.
Production database and test environment should be separated, with no public access to the database.
Blocking malicious websites reduces phishing impact. Built-in Microsoft features keep cost low.
Azure default encryption at rest, disk encryption on laptops and keys stored in Azure Key Vault.
The company develops StoreSight, so secure development rules are needed.
Security and privacy requirements for new features should be written before development.

Control name: Secure system architecture and engineering principles
Justification: Least privilege and private networking guide Azure design.
Secrets must not be in code, and libraries must be kept current.

Justification: Dependency scanning and basic security tests before release. Enterprise customers are likely to ask for evidence.

Control name: Separation of development, test and production environments
Justification: A test environment exists, but production data is sometimes copied into it.
Changes to production go through branch protection and code review.
Test data must be anonymised, not copied from production.

Control name: Protection of information systems during audit testing
Justification: Customer audits and penetration tests must be planned so they do not disrupt production.
